records.text: On June 24, 1374, a "dancing plague" broke out in Aachen.
During the dancing plague, crowds of people danced uncontrollably through the streets for days, some until they collapsed.
The dancing plague was one of several genuinely documented outbreaks of compulsive dancing in medieval Europe.
On June 24, 1497, John Cabot, sailing under an English flag, reached the coast of Newfoundland.
John Cabot became the first European on the North American mainland since the Vikings.
John Cabot was rewarded by King Henry VII with the grand sum of ten pounds.
On June 24, 1717, the first Masonic Grand Lodge in the world, the Premier Grand Lodge of England, was founded in London.
On June 24, 1812, Napoleon led his Grande Armée of around 600,000 men across the Niemen River into Russia.
Less than a tenth of Napoleon's Grande Armée would return from the Russian campaign.
On June 24, 1947, the pilot Kenneth Arnold reported nine objects flying "like a saucer skipping over water" near Mount Rainier.
A newspaper turned Kenneth Arnold's phrasing into "flying saucer".
The modern UFO era was born from the newspaper's coining of the term "flying saucer".
On June 24, 2010, at Wimbledon, John Isner of the United States defeated Nicolas Mahut of France in the longest match in professional tennis history.
The final fifth set of the John Isner vs. Nicolas Mahut match ended 70:68.

An idea from statistical physics: let us train a Markov chain that will gradually turn random noise into the distribution we want.
To do that, let us start with a chain that turns the distribution we want into random noise.
And then let us try to reverse each step.
If we succeed, then later we can start from random noise and move backwards.
Forward diffusion: let us start with p(x0) and add Gaussian noise: q(x_t | x_{t-1}) = N(x_t | √(1 - β_t) x_{t-1}, β_t I).
Then x0 gradually turns into noise, say, in T steps: q(x_{1:T} | x0) = ∏_{t=1}^{T} q(x_t | x_{t-1}).
For each t we can sample x_t in closed form via the reparametrization trick.
Let ϵ ~ N(0, I) and denote α_t = 1 - β_t, A_t = ∏_{i=1}^{T} α_i.
That is, q(x_t | x0) = N(x_t | √A_t x0, (1 - A_t) I).
Because when we add two Gaussians N(0, σ^2_1 I) and N(0, σ^2_2 I), we get a Gaussian N(0, (σ^2_1 + σ^2_2) I).

And now the task, it would seem, is to reverse this process, to learn how to sample from q(x_{t-1} | x_t).

log p_θ(x0) = log p_θ(x0, ..., x_T) - log p_θ(x_1, ..., x_T | x0)

The idea of variational approximations is a very important, fundamental idea in machine learning.
Variational approximations underlie many different models and appear throughout the field.
The derivation of the variational approximation formula begins with the identity p(x,z) = p(x) p(z|x).
Taking logs gives log p(x,z) = log p(x) + log p(z|x).
Rearranging yields log p(x) = log p(x,z) - log p(z|x).
Taking the expectation with respect to any distribution q(z) on both sides gives: log p(x) = E_{q(z)}[log p(x,z) - log p(z|x)].
Since log p(x) does not depend on z, it remains constant under the expectation.
Adding and subtracting E_{q(z)}[log q(z)] (the entropy of q) yields: log p(x) = E_{q(z)}[log p(x,z) - log p(z|x) + log q(z) - log q(z)].
Rearranging terms leads to the formula: log p(x) = E_{q(z)}[log(p(x,z)/p(z))] + E_{q(z)}[log(q(z)/p(z|x))].
That formula is the main formula of variational approximations.
The identity holds for any p(x,z) and any q(z).
On the left side of the formula, log p(x) is a constant.
The goal is to find a distribution q(z) that serves as a good approximation for p(z|x).
The problem is viewed as optimizing a functional with respect to q(z).
On the left side of an equation, there is a term that is independent of q(z) and is the likelihood of the dataset.
On the right side, there is a term L(q) plus the Kullback-Leibler divergence between q(z) and p(z|x).
The Kullback-Leibler divergence is a metric that measures how similar two distributions are.
The KL divergence from Q to P is defined as the integral of Q times log(Q/P) dx.
The KL divergence between q(z) and p(z|x) indicates how close q(z) is to p(z|x).
Minimizing the KL divergence from q(z) to p(z|x) is a good optimization target.
p(z|x) is a very complicated distribution and is hard to work with.
In standard machine learning, p(z|x) is a complicated posterior of a model with many hidden variables requiring integration.
The sum of L(q) and the KL divergence equals a constant that is independent of q(z).
